content:
The objection is old and easy to state. Quran 18:86 says that Dhu al-Qarnayn, travelling west, found the sun setting in a dark or muddy spring.

A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that the sun goes each night to prostrate beneath the Throne and asks leave to rise again.[1] Put together, the critic says, these show an author who pictured a "flat earth" with a sun that travels over it and sinks into the ground.

This article aims to provide context to the charge, insha'Allah, in six answers that keep three things apart: what the Quran's words say, what the hadith says, and how the classical scholars read both. Each charge falls once the texts are read in full.

The verb in 18:86 is wajadahā, "he found it". The verse reports what Dhu al-Qarnayn saw when he reached the western limit of his journey. It makes no statement about where the sun goes.[2]

The classical commentators read it that way. Ibn Kathir explains that the traveller saw the sun as if it were setting into the sea, as anyone standing on a shore sees it. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi argues that the setting cannot be literal, since the earth is round and the sun is far larger than the earth.[3]

The verse describes a sighting, and its earliest expert readers took it as one.

The word for the spring is read in two ways. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hafs read ḥami'a, "muddy". Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Shu'ba read ḥāmiya, "hot".[4]

Al-Tabari records both and the commentators combined them: a hot, dark spring. Either way the word describes what a watcher at the water's edge would see as the sun went down behind it.[4]

The variant changes the colour of the description and leaves its meaning in place.

Ibn Hazm (died 1064) gave a chapter of al-Fisal to the earth being shaped like a ball. He read 39:5, where God "wraps" (yukawwiru) the night over the day, through kawr, the winding of a turban, as night and day wrapping around a globe.[5]

Ibn Taymiyya went further and reported a consensus of the scholars that the heavens and the earth are round, citing Abu al-Husayn ibn al-Munadi (died 947) and Ibn al-Jawzi.[6]

A round earth was the learned Muslim view long before the telescope.

The sun and the moon each "swim in an orbit" (falak), say 21:33 and 36:40. No verse says that the earth is motionless. When 27:61 calls the earth a qarār, the word means a settled place to live.[7]

The verses speak from the viewpoint of a person on the ground, as ordinary speech does, and they describe ordered motion through the heavens.

The text teaches orbits and never a fixed earth.

The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari 3199 and 4802 and Sahih Muslim 159. The Prophet asks Abu Dharr where the sun goes when it sets, and says that it goes to prostrate beneath the Throne and asks permission to rise.[1]

The strongest reading takes the prostration as the submission that the Quran ascribes to everything in creation, including the sun and the moon (22:18; 13:15). On that reading "beneath the Throne" is true at every moment, since the Throne encompasses the whole of creation. Ibn Hajar records such readings in his commentary.[8]

The report then says what the Quran says: the sun moves by its Lord's command and rises by His leave.

Ecclesiastes 1:5 says that the sun rises, sets and hurries back to where it rises. Psalm 19:6 says that it runs its course from one end of the heavens to the other. Weather forecasts today give the times of sunrise and sunset.[9]

The test of a text is whether it lays out a cosmology and asks the reader to believe it. The Quran points to the sun and the moon as signs of order (36:38-40) and does not set out a model of the heavens.[9]

The verse about Dhu al-Qarnayn is the weakest part of the charge, and the commentators answered it centuries ago. The hadith of the prostration, read beside the Quran's account of how all creation bows to God, answers it as well. Our related articles are 4 scientific claims about the Quran that hold up and does a preserved text prove it is true? Allāhu aʿlam.

Notes

  1. Sahih al-Bukhari 3199 and 4802; Sahih Muslim 159 (numbering as on sunnah.com); the hadith texts are on searchtruth.com.
  2. Quran 18:83-90.
  3. Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, ed. Sami ibn Muhammad Salama (Riyadh: Dar Tayba, 1999), vol. 5, p. 191, on 18:86, https://shamela.ws/book/8473/2601; Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, Mafatih al-Ghayb, on 18:86; the al-Razi text is on altafsir.com.
  4. Ibn Mujahid, Kitab al-Sab'a fi al-Qira'at, on 18:86; al-Tabari, Jami al-Bayan (Mecca: Dar al-Tarbiya wa-l-Turath, n.d.; vols. 1–16 ed. Mahmud Muhammad Shakir), vol. 18, p. 95, on 18:86, https://shamela.ws/book/43/10098.
  5. Ibn Hazm, al-Fisal fi al-Milal wa al-Ahwa' wa al-Nihal, part 2, p. 78, the section on the sphericity of the earth (bayān kurawiyyat al-arḍ), in the OpenITI text (JK000343).
  6. Ibn Taymiyya, Majmu' al-Fatawa, ed. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Qāsim (Medina: King Fahd Complex, 1995), vol. 6, p. 586 (the heavens are round, with the consensus reported by Ibn al-Munadi, Ibn Hazm and Ibn al-Jawzi) and vol. 25, p. 195 (Ibn al-Munadi: "there is no disagreement among the scholars that the heaven is like a ball"), in the OpenITI text; Ibn al-Jawzi, Zad al-Masir, on 21:33.
  7. Quran 21:33, 36:38-40, 27:61.
  8. Quran 22:18, 13:15; Ibn Hajar al-'Asqalani, Fath al-Bari sharh Sahih al-Bukhari (Cairo: al-Matba'a al-Salafiyya), vol. 6, pp. 297–300, on Bukhari 3199, https://shamela.ws/book/1673/3491.
  9. Ecclesiastes 1:5; Psalm 19:6; Quran 36:38-40. On reading such verses, Nidhal Guessoum, Islam's Quantum Question (London: I.B. Tauris, 2011).
